## AGENCY:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (“ICE”), Department of Homeland Security (“DHS”); Executive Office for Immigration Review (“EOIR”), Department of Justice (“DOJ”).
## ACTION:
Final rule.
## SUMMARY:

On June 27, 2025, the Departments issued an interim final rule (“IFR”) to streamline assessment of civil penalties under the Immigration and Nationality Act (“INA”) for aliens who fail to depart during a voluntary departure period, willfully fail or refuse to depart after a final removal order and certain other proscribed activities, or are apprehended while improperly entering or attempting to enter the United States. This final rule addresses comments and finalizes the IFR with one change: it permits acceptance of a late-filed appeal based on documented mail delivery delays that ICE finds were beyond the alien's control.
## DATES:
The effective date of this final rule is October 14, 2026.

## SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
## I. Background
## A. Basis and Purpose of the IFR

On January 20, 2025, President Trump issued Executive Order (“E.O.”) 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. E.O. 14159 , 90 FR 8443 (Jan. 29, 2025). In Section 2 of that E.O., President Trump directed that it is “the policy of the United States to faithfully execute the immigration laws against all inadmissible and removable aliens” and “to achieve the total and efficient enforcement of those laws, including through lawful incentives and detention capabilities.” 90 FR 8443 . Section 8 of E.O. 14159 directs the Secretary of Homeland Security, in coordination with the Secretary of the Treasury, to “take all appropriate action to ensure the assessment and collection of all fines and penalties that the Secretary of Homeland Security is authorized by law to assess and collect from aliens unlawfully present in the United States, including aliens who unlawfully entered or unlawfully attempted to enter the United States.” 90 FR 8444-45 . Section 12 of E.O. 14159 directs the Secretary of Homeland Security, in coordination with the Secretary of State and the Attorney General, “to take all appropriate action . . . to adopt policies and procedures to encourage aliens unlawfully in the United States to voluntarily depart as soon as possible, including through enhanced usage of the provisions of section 240B of the INA ( 8 U.S.C. 1229c ), international agreements or assistance, or any other measures that encourage aliens unlawfully in the United States to depart as promptly as possible”. 90 FR 8445 . In Section 2 of E.O. 14165 , Securing Our Borders, President Trump directed the Departments to “take all appropriate action to secure the borders of our Nation,” including by “[d]eterring and preventing the entry of illegal aliens into the United States” and by “[o]btaining complete operational control of the borders of the United States.” E.O. 14165 , 90 FR 8467 (Jan. 30, 2025). In Proclamation 10935, President Trump established Project Homecoming to “present illegal aliens with a choice: either leave the United States voluntarily, with the support and financial assistance of the Federal-government, or face the consequences.” Establishing Project Homecoming, 90 FR 20357 (May 14, 2025).

On June 27, 2025, the Departments issued an IFR, effective on the same date, to streamline how DHS assesses certain civil monetary penalties that Congress has long authorized under the INA. See Imposition and Collection of Civil Penalties for Certain Immigration-Related Violations, 90 FR 27439 (June 27, 2025). The IFR applies to three categories of illegal aliens: (1) aliens who willfully fail or refuse to depart the United States pursuant to a final order of removal or take certain actions to thwart their departure or removal, INA 274D(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1324d(a)(1) ; (2) aliens who voluntarily fail to depart the United States within the time period specified pursuant to a voluntary departure order, INA 240B(d)(1)(A)-(B), 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d)(1)(A)-(B) ;  [ 1 ]

and (3) aliens apprehended while entering (or attempting to enter) the United States unlawfully, INA 275(b)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1325(b)(1) . See also 8 CFR 281.1(a) (scope of the IFR). The IFR revised the Departments' civil monetary penalty procedures for these categories of aliens so that DHS can more efficiently and effectively promote compliance with Immigration Court orders and support border security. See 90 FR 27442 . The IFR partially implements Section 8 of E.O. 14159 and supports DHS's efforts, as directed by the President, to faithfully execute the immigration laws, to achieve total and efficient enforcement of those laws, and to secure the borders of the United States. See 90 FR 27446-47 . The IFR also advances the purpose of Proclamation 10935, Establishing Project Homecoming, by reinforcing that aliens must either voluntarily depart the United States, with Federal support as applicable, or face statutorily authorized consequences for failing to comply with removal or departure orders.

As the IFR explains, the revised procedures are needed to complement DHS's efforts to address the large number of aliens who remain in the United States despite having final removal or voluntary departure orders. See 90 FR 27446 . Prior to the issuance of the IFR, there were approximately 1.5 million aliens on ICE's non-detained docket with final orders of removal, including those who failed to depart after being granted voluntary departure pursuant to INA 240B, 8 U.S.C. 1229c . For example, as discussed in the IFR, in FY 2024 alone, EOIR issued more than 282,000 final removal orders, but DHS data indicate that only about 10 percent of those orders were executed. 90 FR 27445 . In the same year, EOIR granted approximately 8,800 voluntary departure orders, yet only about 50 percent of those aliens confirmed their departure. Id. Moreover, as a result of the prior Administration's policies, including its border policies, the
( printed page 65391)
Immigration Court caseload has dramatically increased in recent years. [ 2 ]

In the third quarter of FY 2026, there were over 3.4 million pending Immigration Court cases, a large percentage of which, if consistent with previous years, will result in removal or voluntary departure orders once adjudicated. [ 3 ]

Thus, without the IFR's intervention, the number of aliens who remain in the United States despite final removal and voluntary departure orders would have been likely to increase in the coming years. Id.

An Immigration Court's order of an alien's removal, unless reversed or vacated on appeal, is binding on all parties, including aliens. See 8 CFR 1240.1(a)(1)(i) , 1240.41 , 1241.1 . Aliens subject to final executable orders of removal  [ 4 ]

remain legally obligated to comply with Immigration Court orders to depart the United States, regardless of prior DHS policies that did not prioritize all such aliens for apprehension, detention, and removal. The large number of unexecuted removal orders and the growth of DHS's non-detained docket demonstrate, however, that many aliens do not comply with this obligation. [ 5 ]

This pattern of large-scale noncompliance risks further encouraging aliens to disregard such orders under the belief that they can remain in the United States without consequence. See 90 FR 27446 . Such noncompliance, in turn, undermines the integrity of the immigration system, weakens the authority of Immigration Courts, and raises fairness concerns for aliens who do comply with removal and departure requirements. See id.

Under this Administration, DHS is taking robust action, consistent with the President's direction, to ramp up efforts to locate, apprehend, detain, and remove aliens with final removal orders who were released under supervision or otherwise not subject to detention in prior years and who remain in the United States. See E.O. 14159 , 90 FR 8443 (Jan. 29, 2025). Managing those removals requires a significant expenditure of ICE resources in addition to costs to taxpayers. [ 6 ]

Although ICE is hiring Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) officers and expanding detention capacity pursuant to additional funding under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Public Law 119-21 , 139 Stat. 72, 358-59 (2025), those efforts will take time to implement, and ICE must continue to devote immigration enforcement resources to all categories of illegal aliens that may or may not be subject to removal orders, including criminal aliens, national security risks, and other aliens unlawfully present in the United States. [ 7 ]

The IFR was also intended to complement DHS's efforts to maintain border security. Under the prior Administration, more than 8 million aliens were encountered along the southern border of the United States. 90 FR 8334 . In FY 2024 alone, DHS estimates that approximately 1.5 million aliens entered or attempted to enter unlawfully between ports of entry. 90 FR 27445 . Although encounters have since declined in connection with this Administration's policies, these prior high encounter levels demonstrate the need for DHS to use all statutorily authorized tools to maintain border security and reduce incentives for unlawful entry. Id.

When such large numbers of aliens enter unlawfully between POEs, as occurred under the last Administration, DHS's capacity to apprehend, process, detain, and swiftly remove all such aliens diminishes. [ 8 ]

As a result, under the prior Administration, millions of aliens were released into communities nationwide, many of whom were subject to but not processed under expedited removal as envisioned by the statutory framework, imposing substantial costs on the States and encouraging additional migration by unlawful aliens who believed they would likely be released into the United States while awaiting removal proceedings that often
( printed page 65392)
take years to resolve. [ 9 ]

When U.S. Border Patrol (“USBP”) officers are diverted from patrol duties to process large groups of migrants and conduct detention-related activities, criminal organizations and smugglers can exploit the diversion of resources to move illegal drugs, weapons, contraband, and aliens into the United States. See E.O. 14165 , 90 FR 8467 (Jan. 20, 2025). Elevated levels of unlawful border crossings also strain ICE's detention resources and impede ICE's ability to detain other aliens, including those with final removal orders. See 90 FR 45397 , 45397 . In combination, the prior Administration's policies and resulting incentives for unlawful entry hindered the effective operation of immigration laws designed to protect U.S. sovereignty and prevent the unlawful entry of illicit contraband, criminals, and illegal aliens.

Additionally, elevated border crossings can severely inhibit the effective functioning of the Immigration Courts. Under the prior Administration, the record numbers of aliens encountered across the southern border overwhelmed DHS's capacity to process such aliens through expedited removal as envisioned by the statutory framework of the Act. 89 FR 81158 . Instead, DHS was forced to place aliens into section 240 removal proceedings at a rate that outpaced EOIR's capacity to complete such cases in a timely manner and led to extensive delays in Immigration Court proceedings. Id. Under this Administration, the Departments have taken significant efforts to disrupt aliens' expectations of lengthy Immigration Court delays, including more robust utilization of expedited removal where available and a renewed focus on EOIR operational efficiency. Accordingly, EOIR has seen a precipitous drop in initial receipts of charging documents to initiate proceedings between FY 2024 and FY 2025, and has been continually increasing the total number of case completions. [ 10 ]

However, considering the challenges experienced under the prior administration at the southern border and the resulting consequences, the Departments have a need to use all available measures to prevent such a situation from reoccurring.

For these reasons, and consistent with this Administration's policies, DHS believes that it must employ all immigration enforcement authorities that Congress has provided in order to both maintain border security, including to discourage large numbers of aliens from crossing the southern border and overwhelming the Departments' abilities to effectively process and remove such aliens as occurred under the last administration, and to address the large number of aliens with removal and voluntary departure orders who have violated U.S. immigration law by remaining in the United States in contravention of such orders.

One such authority is civil monetary penalties. As explained in more detail in the IFR, Congress has authorized DHS to impose civil penalties on: (1) aliens who willfully fail or refuse to depart the United States after a final order of removal or take other action to thwart removal; (2) aliens who fail to comply with a voluntary departure order; and (3) aliens who are apprehended entering or attempting to enter the United States unlawfully (“unlawful entry penalties”). See INA 274D(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1324d(a)(1) ; INA 240B(d)(1)(A), 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d)(1)(A) ; INA 275(b)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1325(b)(1) . Congress has also specified the authorized range of penalty amounts, which DHS has adjusted for inflation. For “unlawful entry,” the penalty amounts range from $100 to $500 per entry or attempted entry. See INA 275(b)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1325(b)(1) ; 8 CFR 280.53(b)(14) . For failure to comply with voluntary departure conditions, the penalty is set by an Immigration Judge or the Board of Immigration Appeals (“BIA”) and may range from $1,992 to $9,970 after inflation adjustments, but the general default amount is $3,000. See INA 240B(d)(1)(A), 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d)(1)(A) ; 8 CFR 280.53(b)(3) , 1240.26 ( l ). For aliens ordered removed who remain in the United States, DHS may impose a penalty of up to $998 for each day the alien willfully fails to comply with the order. See INA 274D(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1324d(a)(1) ; 8 CFR 280.53(b)(14) . As the IFR explains, DHS believes that robust application of these civil penalties will deter future unlawful entries and encourage greater compliance with removal and voluntary departure orders, in line with Congress's intent and this Administration's focus on securing the border and restoring integrity to the immigration system. See 90 FR 27439-40 , 27442 .

Prior to the IFR, however, DHS was required to use the general civil penalty procedures at 8 CFR part 280 to impose these penalties. These procedures were promulgated by the former Immigration and Naturalization Service (“INS”) decades before Congress authorized the specific failure-to-depart and unlawful entry penalties covered by the IFR. See 90 FR 27440-41 . Those regulations were designed primarily for penalties imposed on airlines and other carriers that violate INA provisions governing the transport of aliens into the United States, rather than for penalties against individual aliens for failure-to-depart or unlawful entry. Id. Under those regulations, DHS had to provide a written notice of intent to fine (“NIF”), served in person or by certified mail, and then wait at least 30 days for a response. Id. If the alien did not respond or did not contest the fine, a DHS officer could issue a final decision imposing the penalty. Id. If the alien contested the fine, the alien could request an in-person interview or submit a sworn written response; a supervisory immigration officer would then issue a written decision; the alien could seek reconsideration within DHS; after exhausting DHS procedures, the alien could appeal to the BIA. Id. As discussed in the IFR, these procedures are lengthy, resource intensive, and not tailored to the failure-to-depart and unlawful entry penalties that Congress later authorized. See 90 FR 27444-46 .

The IFR streamlined and simplified the process DHS uses to impose civil penalties for failure-to-depart and unlawful entry and eliminated unnecessary procedures that are not required by statute. See 90 FR 27449-52 . The IFR changed only the way DHS issues and adjudicates civil monetary penalties and the way an alien may contest such penalties for these specific fines. 90 FR 27454 . The IFR did not require the imposition of any new penalties or otherwise change the substantive criteria for issuing civil penalties. Id.

Under the IFR, the new 8 CFR 281 allows a DHS immigration officer to initiate the penalty process by issuing a written decision and order imposing the civil monetary penalty. 8 CFR 281.1(b) , (c) . The decision and order must identify the statutory basis for the penalty, state the type and amount of the penalty, and provide a brief
( printed page 65393)

explanation of the reasons for the decision. 8 CFR 281.1(c)(1) . The decision and order must also advise the alien of the right to appeal; the process for filing an appeal; the right to be represented by counsel at no expense to the government; and the opportunity to submit written arguments and supporting documentation challenging the penalty. 8 CFR 281.1(c)(2) . The alien may file a written defense and supporting evidence or may simply submit a written notice of appeal. 8 CFR 281.1(c)(2) , (e)(1) . DHS may serve the decision and order in person or by regular mail. 8 CFR 281.1(d) .
The IFR also replaced the elaborate review process before DHS set forth in 8 CFR part 280 and appeal process before EOIR set forth at 8 CFR 1280.1   [ 11 ]

for these three specific civil penalties with an appeal process that takes place solely before DHS. Under the IFR, an alien must file a notice of appeal within 15 business days of service of the initial decision and order. 8 CFR 281.1(e)(1) . If the alien does not file a timely appeal with DHS, the initial decision and order become final. 8 CFR 281.1(f)(3) . If the alien files a timely appeal with DHS, a supervisory immigration officer who did not issue the initial decision and order will review the appeal. 8 CFR 281.1(e)(2) . The supervisory officer will review the appeal within 10 days of receipt and may, in his or her discretion, request additional written briefing or documentation, which the alien must provide within 15 days of receiving the request. Id. At the alien's request, the supervisory officer will generally provide copies of pertinent documents and records relevant to the penalty. 8 CFR 281.1(e)(3) . The supervisory officer will decide the appeal on the written record; the IFR does not provide for in-person interviews. Id. The record must include the initial decision and order, evidence in DHS's administrative files, and any timely written submissions, briefs, documentary evidence, or other relevant materials submitted by the alien. Id. The supervisory officer will review this record de novo, including the initial decision and order and any written arguments and evidence submitted by the alien, and will issue a final decision within 45 days. 8 CFR 281.1(e)(2) . That officer's decision constitutes the final agency action, subject only to discretionary review by the Secretary of Homeland Security, and the alien may not appeal the decision to the BIA. 8 CFR 281.1(e)(4) , (f)(1)-(3) . However, the IFR allows DHS to reopen a decision, in its sole discretion ( i.e., sua sponte), at any time to reconsider the decision and reduce or rescind the fine. 8 CFR 281.1(f)(1) .

As explained in the IFR, the Departments reasoned that these updated procedures will allow DHS to impose these civil penalties more swiftly on more aliens who unlawfully enter the United States and on those who disregard removal and voluntary departure orders. See 90 FR 27442 . In turn, this will help support DHS's efforts to maintain border security and enforce immigration laws by deterring unlawful entries and encouraging compliance with removal and departure orders. See 90 FR 27445-46 . Compared to the general procedures in 8 CFR part 280 , the revised process reduces unnecessary administrative burdens and allows DHS to reach final decisions more quickly while at the same time reducing unnecessary burdens on the BIA's caseload. See 90 FR 27444-45 . The IFR explained that these changes are needed to ensure that DHS can efficiently employ these statutory penalties while continuing to prioritize, without diverting resources away from, border security and the apprehension, detention, and removal of aliens who have violated the Nation's immigration laws, consistent with this Administration's policy objectives and the President's direction. See 90 FR 27444-46 .

To further advance the IFR's goal of encouraging compliance with removal and departure orders, DHS has announced that it will rescind most failure to depart fines if an alien uses the U.S. Customs and Border Protection (“CBP”) Home app to arrange and complete self-departure from the United States. [ 12 ]

This policy, coupled with DHS's expanded use of these civil penalties, is intended to provide an additional clear incentive for aliens to comply with removal and departure orders and avoid civil monetary penalties by doing what the law requires: departing the United States as ordered. [ 13 ]

At the same time, the Departments determined that the revised procedures are consistent with due process. For the reasons discussed more fully in the IFR and in response to comments in Section III of this preamble, the Departments have concluded that a shortened appeal period, removal of in-person interviews, and the shift from BIA review to internal DHS review are appropriate and consistent with due process given that these civil penalties typically turn on routine and straightforward factual and legal determinations and aliens have limited grounds to contest them. 90 FR 27451-55 . In addition, ICE will now also permit acceptance of a late-filed appeal based on documented mail delivery delays that ICE finds were beyond the alien's control.

First, INA 275(b), 8 U.S.C. 1325(b) , authorizes DHS to impose a civil penalty on any alien who is apprehended while entering or attempting to enter the United States at an improper place or time. Aliens apprehended while entering unlawfully have, by definition, violated INA 275(b), 8 U.S.C. 1325(b) , and the documented encounter provides the only fact necessary to impose these penalties. Additionally, when USBP agents apprehend an alien entering unlawfully, the agents prepare a Form I-213, Record of Deportable/Inadmissible Alien, which documents the apprehension and is sufficient to demonstrate liability for these penalties. See 90 FR 27442 . As a matter of practice, USBP issues these penalties at the time that it apprehends the alien. In these circumstances, the Departments do not believe that a lengthy, multi-step appeal process is necessary. See id. The IFR's appeal structure preserves an alien's meaningful ability to contest an unlawful entry penalty if the alien believes a penalty was issued erroneously.

Second, the nature of the failure to depart penalties also supports the IFR's changes. Congress has authorized DHS to impose civil monetary penalties on aliens for failure to depart, subject to the general federal statute of limitations, 28
( printed page 65394)

U.S.C. 2462, if two elements have been satisfied: (1) the alien is subject to a final order of removal or was granted voluntary departure and (2) the alien willfully fails or refuses to depart under a removal order or voluntarily fails to comply with a voluntary departure order. INA 274D(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1324d(a)(1) ; INA 240B(d)(1)(A), 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d)(1)(A) . DHS maintains records of an alien's immigration history, including removal and voluntary departure orders, and has ready access to information about any pending appeals needed to verify that the alien is subject to a final removal or departure order. 90 FR 27442-43 . Before issuing a penalty, ICE guidance requires the immigration officer to verify that there are no DHS records of the alien's departure from the United States and reviews the alien's immigration records for information suggesting that the alien's failure to depart was not willful or voluntary. This includes information about: automatic stays resulting from motions to reopen; certain immigration benefits under the Violence Against Women Act (“VAWA”) that stay the alien's removal; for aliens on an order of supervision, efforts the alien has made to secure travel documents at DHS's request; whether DHS has affirmatively approved the alien for deferred action; whether the Immigration Courts, DHS, or a federal court has granted a stay of removal; and whether DHS or EOIR has granted the alien protection that excuses the alien's failure to depart while the alien maintains that protection, including temporary protected status (“TPS”), protection under the Convention Against Torture (“CAT”), and withholding of removal under INA 241(b)(3), 8 U.S.C. 1231(b)(3) when no alternative country of removal is available.

Absent evidence in records accessible to DHS showing that the alien is permitted to remain in the United States, or that the alien has departed, DHS believes the statutory prerequisites to issue a penalty will have been met where an alien ordered removed or granted voluntary departure is physically present in the United States beyond the time frame specified by the Immigration Judge. As the IFR explains, civil penalties for failure to depart are generally issued after completion of section 240 removal proceedings that resulted in a final order requiring the alien's departure from the United States immediately or within a certain time frame specified by the Immigration Judge. See 90 FR 27440 . These aliens have received due process through section 240 removal proceedings where they had an opportunity to contest the charges against them, to seek relief, and to be informed by an Immigration Judge of their obligation to depart and of the consequences of failing to do so. Id. Aliens granted voluntary departure prior to the conclusion of section 240 removal proceedings have already agreed to forgo challenging removal or seeking relief in exchange for being allowed to depart voluntarily. Id. In these circumstances, and when DHS records show the removal order is executable, the Departments reasoned that an alien's continued presence in the United States is generally sufficient to establish liability for these civil penalties, absent the alien providing evidence on appeal  [ 14 ]
to demonstrate otherwise. See 90 FR 27442-43 .

In addition, Immigration Judges are required by law to inform aliens of their departure obligations and the consequences for failing to comply. Under INA 240(c)(5), 8 U.S.C. 1229(a)(5) , when an Immigration Judge orders removal, the Immigration Judge must inform the alien of the consequences for failure to depart under the order of removal, including civil penalties described at sections INA 274D, 8 U.S.C. 1324(d) . See 8 CFR 1240.13(d) . Likewise, for voluntary departure, the INA requires that an Immigration Judge “shall inform the alien of the penalties” that will apply if the alien voluntarily fails to depart within the time allowed, including civil monetary penalties and ineligibility for certain forms of relief. INA 240B(d)(3), 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d)(3) . These advisals are mandatory components of 240 removal proceedings, not discretionary steps.

These statutory and regulatory requirements are directly relevant to the willfulness and voluntariness elements in the civil penalty statutes. Before DHS considers imposing a failure to depart penalty, the alien will ordinarily have been advised, on the record, that the law requires the alien to depart the United States and that failure to do so may result in civil fines and other adverse consequences. When an alien remains in the United States after such clear, legally required notice, his or her continued presence strongly supports the conclusion that the alien has “willfully fail[ed] or refuse[d]” to depart under a removal order or “voluntarily” failed to comply with a voluntary departure order, as required by the failure to depart civil penalty statutes. In making this assessment, DHS also relies on the presumption of regularity that attaches to official acts of government officers, including Immigration Judges. See United States Postal Serv. v. Gregory, 534 U.S. 1, 10 (2001). Under this presumption, DHS may reasonably assume that Immigration Judges complied with their legal obligations under the INA and implementing regulations and provided the required advisals concerning departure obligations and the consequences of noncompliance, absent specific evidence to the contrary in the record. In all cases, ICE considers the willfulness of an alien's violation in determining whether to impose a penalty.

Taken together—(1) the procedural protections provided in section 240 removal proceedings, (2) the mandatory Immigration Judge advisals of departure obligations and penalties, (3) the presumption of regularity applicable to those advisals, and (4) DHS's careful review of U.S. Government records to confirm that the alien is subject to a final, executable order and lacks lawful permission to remain—DHS concludes that an alien's continued presence in the United States is generally sufficient to establish the willful or voluntary failure to depart required to impose these civil penalties, absent evidence provided by the alien on appeal to demonstrate that the alien is not liable. Therefore, the Departments reasoned that streamlining the issuance and adjudication of these civil penalties, and the associated appeals process, aligns more closely with the nature and intent of these straightforward civil penalties. While in most cases, DHS records sufficiently establish the facts necessary to demonstrate that the alien is subject to these civil penalties, the alien retains the right to contest them on limited grounds. See 90 FR 27442-46 .

To the extent an alien believes that DHS issued a penalty erroneously—for example, because the alien is not subject to a removal order, is legally permitted to remain in the United States, or did not willfully or voluntarily fail to depart—the Departments determined that the IFR provides sufficient notice and an opportunity to contest the decision before DHS, and that further review before EOIR is unnecessary. See 90 FR 27451-55 . Under the IFR, a DHS immigration officer must issue a written decision that sets forth the statutory and factual basis for the penalty and informs the alien of the requirements and deadlines for filing an appeal. See Mullane v. Cent. Hanover Bank & Tr. Co., 339 U.S. 306, 314 (1950) (stating
( printed page 65395)

that notice under due process must be of a sufficient nature as to reasonably convey the required information). The revised appeal process also preserves an alien's opportunity to contest a civil penalty. Under the IFR's procedures, the alien has 15 business days to appeal using the DHS-developed Form 281, Notice and Violation of Order, and a supervisory immigration officer who did not issue the initial decision will review the record de novo and may request additional evidence before making a final determination. See 90 FR 27452-54 .

As explained in the IFR and in response to comments in Section III of this preamble, the Departments believe that additional procedures, beyond those contained in the IFR, would not enhance the accuracy, fairness, or reliability of the process given the straightforward nature of these penalties and the limited grounds that an alien may have to contest them. See id. Thus, for the reasons discussed in the IFR and in response to comments in Section III of this preamble, the Departments believe that the revised procedure preserves an alien's ability to contest the fine while better ensuring that the BIA does not unnecessarily expend resources in areas where DHS is better positioned to review such determinations, and that DHS can reach final decisions efficiently and apply these statutory penalties swiftly and at the scale necessary to address the large number of aliens who have entered or remain unlawfully in the United States. Accordingly, after carefully considering comments received on the IFR, the Departments are finalizing this rule with one change discussed in more detail below to account for U.S. postal delays.
## B. The Departments' Experience With the IFR

The IFR is working as intended. As a result of the IFR, DHS has been able to issue a significantly greater number of civil penalties compared to the pre-IFR process under 8 CFR part 280 . From March 26, 2025, through June 26, 2025, ICE issued 12,135 civil penalties under the pre-IFR process. [ 15 ]

From June 27, 2025, after the IFR took effect, through September 14, 2026, ICE issued approximately 110,000 failure to depart civil penalties, and CBP issued an additional 66,000 civil penalties for unlawful entry. Thus, DHS increased the number of civil penalties issued from approximately 930 per week under the pre-IFR process to nearly 2,800 per week under the IFR process. [ 16 ]

Accordingly, the IFR has allowed DHS to impose more civil penalties more quickly on a greater scale, while retaining procedural safeguards designed to promote accurate penalty assessments without diverting resources away from border security, and the apprehension, detention, and removal of aliens who have violated our immigration laws.

Second, DHS's robust use of civil penalties appears to be shifting incentives for aliens with removal and departure orders who might otherwise remain unlawfully in the United States. DHS data indicates that over 82,000 aliens with removal orders and voluntary departures orders have self-departed from the United States since DHS began issuing civil penalties in March 2025 through September 14, 2026. [ 17 ]
In that same period, over 7,700 aliens have self-departed after receiving a civil penalty. [ 18 ]

Further, the number of aliens with removal orders or voluntary departure orders who have self-departed since the IFR took effect has increased significantly, as has the number of aliens who have departed after receiving a civil penalty. In the pre-IFR period from March 26, 2025, through June 26, 2025, approximately 8,600 aliens with removal or voluntary departure orders self-departed, and approximately 540 aliens self-departed the United States after receiving a civil penalty during this period. [ 19 ]

In the post-IFR period from June 27, 2025, through September 14, 2026, over 74,000 aliens with removal orders or voluntary departure orders self-departed in total, and approximately 7,180 aliens self-departed after receiving a civil penalty during this period. This data indicates that DHS's robust use of civil penalties, as facilitated by the IFR's streamlined procedures, is encouraging illegally present aliens to depart the United States on their own, consistent with the IFR's objectives.

Finally, DHS's experience implementing the civil penalties covered by this rule since March 26, 2025, confirms that many pre-IFR procedures were unnecessary and that the IFR's procedures provide a meaningful opportunity to contest penalties believed to be erroneous without unnecessarily diverting BIA resources away from adjudicating its existing pending caseload to conduct review better addressed by DHS. As discussed above, the IFR shortens the appeal period, eliminates in-person interviews, and shifts appeals from the BIA to DHS. DHS data support these changes:

• Under the pre-IFR process, aliens filed written answers pursuant to 8 CFR 280.12 contesting failure to depart penalties for only 222 of the 12,135 notices of intent to fine that ICE issued, a less than 2 percent appeal rate. Under the post-IFR process through September 10, 2026, aliens appealed failure to depart civil penalties in 3,072 cases of the approximately 110,000 penalties that ICE issued between June 27, 2025, through September 14, 2026, a nearly 3 percent appeal rate. The appeal rate has therefore increased under the post-IFR process. [ 20 ]

• Only 4 aliens requested an in-person interview out of the 222 penalty notices that aliens contested under the pre-IFR process, indicating that in-person interviews are generally unnecessary and that aliens can adequately contest these decisions through written submissions based on information in the alien's possession.

• Under the pre-IFR process, only 44 aliens appealed DHS's penalty decision to the BIA under 8 CFR part 1003 , further supporting the Departments' assessment that the legal issues associated with these penalties are relatively straightforward and appeals can be handled by DHS. As of September 10, 2026, the BIA has issued only two decisions in these appeals, including a published decision which
( printed page 65396)
upheld the civil penalty. [ 21 ]
This further supports the Departments' decision to eliminate BIA review in favor of an internal DHS appeal process given the lengthy BIA adjudication timeframes.

• Aliens have successfully contested penalty decisions under the post-IFR processes. Of the appeals that DHS has adjudicated under the post-IFR process, aliens prevailed in 25 percent of the cases. This clearly demonstrates that the IFR's appeal process is meaningful, and DHS can adjudicate these penalties fairly without the need for the BIA's review.

These results support the Departments' conclusion that the IFR's streamlined procedures provide appropriate protections while allowing DHS to apply statutory penalties efficiently and at scale. DHS believes there have been fewer appeals to fines issued under 8 CFR part 281 , as compared to 8 CFR part 280 , because of the straightforward determinations of fact associated with fines under part 281. Additionally, the appeal process under 8 CFR part 281 discourages frivolous or non-meritorious appeals, focusing resources on cases with substantive claims.
## II. Statutory Authority

The Attorney General and Secretary of Homeland Security issue this joint final rule pursuant to their respective authorities. The Homeland Security Act of 2002 (“HSA”), Public Law 107-296 , 116 Stat. 2135, as amended, transferred to the Secretary many functions previously exercised by the former INS in implementing and enforcing Federal immigration law. The INA, as amended, charges the Secretary “with the administration and enforcement of this chapter and all other laws relating to the immigration and naturalization of aliens.” INA 103(a)(1); 8 U.S.C. 1103(a)(1) . It authorizes the Secretary to take actions “necessary for carrying out” that responsibility. INA 103(a)(3); 8 U.S.C. 1103(a)(3) . As relevant here, the INA and HSA now authorize the Secretary to impose most civil monetary penalties under the INA, including those set forth in INA 240B(d), 274D(a), and 275(b); 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d) , 1324d(a) , and 1325(b) . See INA 103(a)(1); 8 U.S.C. 1103(a)(1) (reposing in the Secretary the authority to administer and enforce the immigration laws except as expressly reserved to the President, Attorney General, or Secretary of State) and HSA 402(3), 6 U.S.C. 202(3) (charging the Secretary with carrying out the immigration enforcement functions vested by statute in, or performed by, the Commissioner of the former INS).

Within DHS, the HSA allocated immigration functions and responsibilities to CBP, ICE, and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (“USCIS”). See HSA 411, 6 U.S.C. 211 (CBP); HSA 442, 6 U.S.C. 252 (ICE); HSA 451, 6 U.S.C. 271 (USCIS). ICE is generally responsible for interior immigration enforcement, and CBP is generally responsible for immigration enforcement at ports of entry and along the United States border. Both components have authority to administer civil monetary penalties relating to certain violations of immigration law and Immigration Court orders, including penalties authorized under INA 240B(d), 274(D)(a), and 275(b). See, e.g., 8 CFR part 280 .

The Secretary may delegate or re-delegate any authority vested in DHS under the immigration laws to any DHS officer, official, or employee, including by successive delegations. See INA 103(a)(4), 8 U.S.C. 1103(a)(4) ; 8 CFR 2.1 ; Authority of the Secretary of Homeland Security; Immigration Laws, 68 FR 10922 (Mar. 6, 2003). The Secretary may delegate his authority in any manner he chooses, including by regulation, memorandum, directive, or other method. 8 CFR 2.1 . In addition, HSA 102(a)(3), 6 U.S.C. 112(a)(3) , vests all functions of DHS officers, employees, and organizational units in the Secretary.

The HSA retains in DOJ, under the direction of the Attorney General, the functions of EOIR. See HSA 1101, 6 U.S.C. 521 , INA 103(g)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1103(g)(1) . Immigration Judges within EOIR conduct section 240 removal proceedings and have authority to issue removal orders or grant voluntary departure. See INA 240, 240B, 8 U.S.C. 1229a , 1229b . The INA further provides that the Attorney General's determinations on questions of law “shall be controlling.” INA 103(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1103(a)(1) . Nothing in this final rule alters EOIR's or the Attorney General's authority to conduct or review section 240 removal proceedings, including the issuance of removal orders or grants of voluntary departure.

DOJ participates in this rulemaking because, prior to the IFR, DOJ's regulations established BIA appellate jurisdiction over certain DHS-issued civil monetary penalties authorized under the INA, including those covered by this rulemaking. The IFR removed that appellate authority, which is finalized without further change in this rule. See 90 FR 27439 , 27459 . The INA does not require the BIA to review civil penalties, and nothing in the statute precludes the Attorney General from removing the BIA's appellate jurisdiction over civil monetary penalties imposed by another agency. To the contrary, INA 103(g)(1) and (g)(2), 8 U.S.C. 1103(g)(1)-(2) , authorize the Attorney General to issue regulations necessary for carrying out EOIR's responsibilities and governing its adjudicatory structure. Consistent with that authority, through the IFR, DOJ amended its regulations to eliminate the BIA's appellate authority over these DHS-imposed penalties in order to focus EOIR's resources on its statutory functions.

This final rule addresses DHS procedures for imposing civil monetary penalties under INA 240B(d), 274D(a)(1), and 275(b), 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d) , 1324d(a) , and 1325(b) . Those statutory provisions define the categories of aliens subject to civil penalties, establish penalty amounts, and authorize DHS to impose such penalties, but they do not prescribe procedures DHS must follow or require DOJ review of those penalties. Similarly, INA 280, 8 U.S.C. 1330 , addresses the collection of civil monetary penalties but does not specify assessment procedures. Accordingly, the INA affords DHS discretion to adopt reasonable procedures for assessing and issuing civil monetary penalties. See Vt. Yankee Nuclear Power Corp. v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 435 U.S. 519, 543 (1978) (“Absent constitutional constraints or extremely compelling circumstances the administrative agencies should be free to fashion their own rules of procedure and to pursue methods of inquiry capable of permitting them to discharge their multitudinous duties.”) (cleaned up).
## III. Response to Public Comments on the IFR

The Departments received a total of 28 public comment submissions in response to the IFR. The Departments reviewed all the public comments received and have addressed relevant comments in this final rule, grouped by subject matter. While some commenters wrote that they supported the IFR, the vast majority of commenters opposed all or part of it.
## A. General Support

Comment: Several commenters expressed overall support for the IFR. These commenters agreed with the use of civil monetary penalties to promote compliance with immigration laws. One commenter considered such civil penalties necessary to deter unlawful presence, encourage self-departure, and help offset the costs associated with
( printed page 65397)

enforcing immigration laws and carrying out removals. Another commenter recognized the government's interest in recovering some of the costs associated with removing aliens. A third commenter expressed general support for imposing civil monetary fines to strengthen overall immigration enforcement. Collectively, these comments broadly endorsed the IFR's underlying policy objective of streamlining the process for imposing civil monetary penalties on aliens subject to the violations addressed in this rule.

Response: The Departments agree that promoting compliance with the Nation's immigration laws and maintaining border security is critical, and this rule is a key part of DHS's efforts to use all statutorily available tools to help achieve those objectives consistent with the Administration's policies and priorities while also allowing EOIR to focus time and resources on completing cases that are more aligned with its statutory authorities. See 90 FR 8445-55 . Specifically, the unprecedented number of aliens entering and remaining in the country illegally, in recent years necessitates this rule. See 90 FR 27442 (quoting 90 FR 8443 ). Congress has authorized DHS to impose civil monetary penalties on aliens who unlawfully enter the United States and those who remain after a final removal or voluntary departure order. See 90 FR 27439-41 . As explained in the IFR, this rule allows DHS to preserve due process while more efficiently imposing a greater number of these civil penalties on the aliens subject to them. 90 FR 27442 . The Departments believe that this effort will, in turn, encourage greater compliance with removal and voluntary departure orders and discourage future unlawful entries. Id.
## B. General Opposition
## 1. Impacts on Aliens, Families, Businesses, and Communities

Comment: Many commenters opposed the IFR, asserting that it will negatively impact aliens and their families. One commenter stated that the aliens impacted by this rule could face steep civil monetary fines in excess of $1,000,000, causing significant financial distress for them and their families. Other commenters echoed this point, stating that the rule creates a substantial financial burden on aliens, and specifically viewed as particularly egregious the fine of $998-per-day for willful failure or refusal to depart after a final removal order and certain other proscribed activities. One commenter said the IFR directly harms U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents because many aliens subject to these civil monetary fines are parents and spouses of U.S. citizens and permanent residents. They characterized these fines as “economically catastrophic for the entire household” resulting in “eviction, bankruptcy, or forced separation.” This commenter also noted that aliens who fail to pay the assessed penalties may be subject to additional consequences including garnished wages, seizure of assets including homes and vehicles, and long-term financial ruin.

Another commenter reiterated this point and additionally noted the potential confiscation of savings and vehicles and imposed additional financial planning burden and financial uncertainty. This commenter claimed that the Departments' conclusion that the IFR aligns with due process was arbitrary and capricious. The commenter said that the IFR arbitrarily characterized these penalties as “modest,” and claimed the Departments overlooked case law recognizing heightened due process interests when the government seizes homes, confiscates savings, and imposes fines that result in significant economic impacts on families. Given the substantial penalty amounts and the collateral consequences that can result if an alien fails to pay, the commenter argued that the IFR's procedures are constitutionally inadequate.

Response: As an initial point, Congress, not the Departments, has defined both the types of violations and the monetary range for the civil penalties covered by the IFR and this rule. These penalties and their amounts reflect Congress's judgment that the conduct involved—an alien's unlawful entry and failure to depart after a removal or voluntary departure order—is serious, and in some cases substantial civil fines are necessary to encourage aliens to comply with the immigration laws. See 90 FR 27439-40 . This rule does not expand the scope of these penalties, nor their minimum or maximum dollar amounts. Furthermore, the immigration consequences for failing to depart or unlawful entry flow from the underlying immigration violation, not from the failure to pay the assessed civil monetary penalties. This rule merely streamlines the process that DHS applies when imposing civil penalties that Congress has already authorized DHS to impose. Therefore, to the extent that commenters are objecting to these civil monetary penalties and the amounts authorized by Congress, such concerns are outside of the scope of this rulemaking.

DHS often assesses the maximum penalty amount to fulfill the enforcement and deterrent objectives of the statute, as intended by Congress. These amounts are also consistent with the enforcement priorities of the Administration, as reflected in recent Executive Orders. See 90 FR 8443 , 8443-45 ; 90 FR 8467 , 8467 . However, the Departments note that, in the voluntary departure context, immigration officers follow the civil penalty amounts that will continue to be set by EOIR. See 8 CFR 1240.26 ( l ).

The Departments disagree with commenters' arguments that DHS should not streamline the process for imposing these civil penalties because of the burdens the penalties create for aliens and their families. The Departments acknowledge these concerns but note that financial, emotional, and family burdens are also an inherent consequence of removal based on an alien's violation of the Nation's immigration laws. See e.g., Moctezuma-Reyes v. Garland, 124 F.4th 416, 423 (6th Cir. 2024) (“[F]inancial and emotional strains are the typical results of removal; they aren't rare”); see also Matter of Pilch, 21 I&N Dec. 627, 631 (BIA 1996) (“[E]motional hardship caused by severing family and community ties is a common result of deportation”). The most substantial civil fines apply only to aliens who have been ordered removed or granted voluntary departure after the conclusion of immigration proceedings. These aliens have been warned of the consequences for failing to comply with the removal or departure order but have willfully ignored their departure obligations. In these circumstances, the Departments do not believe that it is unfair to impose substantial civil penalties that Congress has authorized for these violations even though it may cause additional burdens and hardships on aliens and their families.

To help alleviate the financial burden of civil penalties and incentivize compliance, DHS has announced it will reopen and rescind most outstanding civil penalties when an alien uses the CBP Home app to voluntarily self-depart the United States. [ 22 ]
This option allows aliens to avoid the civil penalties and attendant consequences that commenters have noted. The
( printed page 65398)

Departments recognize that an alien's choice to exercise this option may still impose significant personal and family hardships, including to U.S. citizen or lawful permanent family members, but the Departments note that these hardships are an inherent consequence of a removal order and are compounded by the alien's willful failure to depart when that order became final and executable. See Morales-Izquierdo v. DHS, 600 F.3d 1076, 1091 (9th Cir. 2010) (rejecting argument that “an illegal alien with United States citizen family members cannot be removed” because such a proposition “would radically alter the status quo of our immigration law”). Additionally, the Departments believe that permitting removable aliens to remain in the United States would undermine immigration enforcement, the integrity of the Nation's immigration laws, American communities, and public safety. [ 23 ]

Regarding commenters' concerns that aliens may face collateral consequences if they fail to take advantage of this off-ramp and further fail to pay these civil fines, the Departments note that the IFR and this final rule do not authorize the confiscation of savings, garnished wages, or the seizure of assets. Rather, separate statutes and regulations govern the U.S. Government's debt collection activities and remedies, which are outside the scope of this rule. However, the Departments note that only DOJ's Civil Division or another authorized litigating component of DOJ, not EOIR and DHS, have authority to obtain a judgment on a debt owed to the United States. See 31 CFR 904.1-904.4 . DOJ's Civil Division or another authorized litigating component must bring an action in federal court to obtain a judgment and pursue any lien against assets or confiscation of savings, and the alien has an opportunity to request a federal court hearing on the enforceability of the debt. See, e.g., 28 U.S.C. 3002(3)(B) , 3101(d)(1) , (d)(2). This provides due process before the U.S. Government seeks to obtain a judgment on an uncollected debt and before it can confiscate an alien's property or savings. Accordingly, nothing in this rule deprives an alien of the ability to challenge the imposition of particular civil penalty assessments or collection methods that the alien regards as disproportionate, excessive, or in violation of due process during a federal court hearing.

Finally, the Departments disagree that the IFR's due process analysis fails to consider the full magnitude of the departure penalties and the collateral consequences that could result, should an alien remain in the United States and fail to pay the civil monetary penalty. As an initial matter, contrary to one commenter's claim, the Departments did not characterize the penalties covered by this rule as “modest.” Rather, the IFR used that term to contrast the penalty amounts associated with the unlawful entry and voluntary departure order penalties and the per diem fines Congress has authorized DHS to impose on aliens who willfully remain in the United States for many years after a removal order. See 90 FR 27541 .

The Departments do, however, acknowledge that the per diem civil penalties can result in substantial fines, including sums of over one million dollars in certain cases, and that these amounts could impose significant economic and emotional burdens on aliens and their families. The Departments also note that DHS will cancel most outstanding penalties when an alien uses the CBP Home app to depart the United States, as discussed above. Similarly, the Departments acknowledge the collateral consequences that could result if an alien fails to pay a civil penalty or depart the United States, but the Departments reiterate that this rule does not authorize DHS or EOIR to seize an alien's property, garnish wages, or confiscate savings. That authority rests with DOJ's Civil Division or another litigating component, and the alien would be able to challenge any action in court before any deprivation occurs.

The Departments, however, also have a weighty interest in ensuring that DHS can impose statutorily authorized civil monetary penalties efficiently and at scale to create greater incentives for aliens to comply with final removal orders and to impose timely consequences on those who do not. As the Departments explained in the IFR and Section II of this preamble, the need for this rule is demonstrated by the sheer number of aliens in the United States with final removal orders and the risk that, without additional action, a significant number of the millions of aliens currently in Immigration Court proceedings may be encouraged to simply ignore final decisions ordering their removal. See 90 FR 27445 . An alien's failure to comply with a removal order risks undermining the overall integrity of the immigration laws and processes and imposes significant enforcement costs on DHS. Id; see also Section II of this preamble.

On balance, the Departments believe that the IFR's streamlined civil monetary penalty procedures strike an appropriate balance between: (1) increasing DHS's ability to impose statutorily authorized civil penalties quickly against aliens who have willfully failed to comply with removal orders and (2) protecting an alien's interest in ensuring that he or she has a meaningful opportunity to contest any civil penalty that DHS may have issued erroneously. Based on its experience, DHS believes that the risk of imposing these civil fines in error is low given the straightforward nature of these civil penalty determinations, and that the IFR's procedures provide sufficient due process to aliens who contest these penalties. See 90 FR 27451-54 .

Comment: Commenters claimed that these penalties will harm businesses and communities. One commenter stated that many aliens targeted by this IFR pay taxes and work in “essential” sectors such as agriculture, healthcare, and construction. Another commenter claimed that the threat of high civil penalties will increase fear in communities and push people into hiding. The commenter claimed that the high penalties would reduce enrollment in schools and healthcare, and deter victims and witnesses from reporting crimes, thereby harming public safety and communities. Given these claimed impacts, commenters argued that the Departments should rescind the IFR.

Response: The Departments do not dispute the contributions of lawful immigrants to United States businesses and communities. The purpose of the IFR and this rule, however, is not to harm businesses or communities but to allow DHS to more efficiently impose these statutorily authorized civil monetary penalties on the large number of aliens who violate the Nation's immigration laws by entering or remaining in the country unlawfully. Congress has authorized DHS to impose civil penalties for these violations and did not create exceptions for aliens who pay taxes, work in “essential sectors”, or otherwise “contribute” to communities. An alien's engagement in these activities does not absolve him or her from complying with the immigration laws. Moreover, the Departments note that, with limited exceptions, Congress has not authorized
